html:
The appearance of the Indian monk Swami Vivekananda at the World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago in September 1893, which introduced Hindu thought to a large Western audience.

The Parliament was held alongside the World's Columbian Exposition, a great fair marking 400 years since Columbus. Vivekananda, a disciple of the Bengali mystic Ramakrishna, had travelled with little money and no formal invitation. On the opening day, 11 September, he began his short speech with "Sisters and brothers of America", and the hall rose in applause. He spoke of tolerance and of all religions as paths to the same truth.

He stayed in the West for several years, lecturing across the United States and in Britain, and founded the Vedanta Society of New York in 1894. He presented Vedanta and yoga as a rational, universal spirituality. Anagarika Dharmapala spoke for Buddhism at the same gathering. Back in India in 1897, Vivekananda was greeted as a hero and founded the Ramakrishna Mission. His success gave Indians new confidence in their culture, and in India 11 September is remembered for his speech.
sum: The appearance of the Indian monk Swami Vivekananda at the World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago in September 1893, which introduced Hindu thought to a large Western audience.
